title: What BSA training does the NCUA require of credit unions?
description: NCUA rule 12 CFR 748.2 requires every federally insured credit union's BSA program to train appropriate personnel. What that means, and the 2026 proposal.
shortAnswer: The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) requires every federally insured credit union to run a written Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, approved by its board, that at a minimum provides training for appropriate personnel. The rule is 12 CFR 748.2(c)(4), and NCUA examiners must review the program at every examination. A 2026 interagency proposal would restate the requirement as an ongoing employee training program; as at November 2026 it is not final.
keyTakeaways: 12 CFR 748.2(c) sets four minimum program elements for federally insured credit unions: internal controls, independent testing, a designated BSA individual, and "training for appropriate personnel".

The program must be written, approved by the board of directors, and reflected in the minutes (748.2(b)(1)), and the credit union's president or managing official certifies compliance with Part 748 annually in the Credit Union Profile (748.1(a)).
The Federal Credit Union Act, 12 U.S.C. 1786(q)(2), requires every NCUA examination to include a review of BSA compliance procedures and the exam report to describe any problem.
NCUA and the other agencies endorse collaborative arrangements that let smaller credit unions share BSA resources, including training, with other institutions.

On April 10, 2026 the NCUA, OCC and FDIC proposed rewriting 748.2 as an AML/CFT program rule with an "ongoing employee training program"; comments closed June 9, 2026, and the current rule still applies.
regulator: National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) as administrator of the Bank Secrecy Act; state supervisory authorities for state-chartered credit unions
appliesTo: Credit union boards of directors, which approve the BSA program
BSA officers, member-facing staff, lending, operations and audit personnel in credit unions

sections.heading: What does 12 CFR 748.2 require for BSA training?

blocks.text: It requires each federally insured credit union's BSA compliance program to "provide training for appropriate personnel", as one of four minimum elements. [12 CFR 748.2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-VII/subchapter-A/part-748/section-748.2) implements the Federal Credit Union Act's direction that credit unions maintain procedures reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA, and it has not been amended since 2011.

blocks.title: 12 CFR 748.2(c): contents of compliance program
blocks.text: "Such compliance program shall at a minimum: (1) Provide for a system of internal controls to assure ongoing compliance; (2) Provide for independent testing for compliance to be conducted by credit union personnel or outside parties; (3) Designate an individual responsible for coordinating and monitoring day-to-day compliance; and (4) Provide training for appropriate personnel."

Two governance requirements frame the training element. Under 748.2(b)(1) the program "must be written, approved by the credit union's board of directors, and reflected in the credit union's minutes." Under 748.2(b)(2) the customer identification program in 31 CFR 1020.220 is part of the BSA program, so staff who open accounts need training on it. Because FinCEN's rules treat credit unions as banks, the bank program rule in 31 CFR 1020.210 applies as well; that framework is explained on the [Bank Secrecy Act AML training](/regulations/bsa-aml-training-requirements) page.

sections.heading: How does the NCUA check BSA training?

blocks.text: Every NCUA examination includes a review of the credit union's BSA procedures, and training is part of what examiners test. [12 U.S.C. 1786(q)(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title12/html/USCODE-2024-title12-chap14-subchapII-sec1786.htm) requires that each examination "include a review of the procedures" and that the report "describe any problem with the procedures maintained by the credit union." Under 1786(q)(3), failing to establish the procedures, or failing to fix a previously reported problem, leads to a cease and desist order.

The NCUA's [BSA and AML resources page](https://ncua.gov/regulation-supervision/regulatory-compliance-resources/bank-secrecy-act-resources) states that "all credit unions must comply with BSA regulations" and directs credit unions to the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) BSA/AML Examination Manual, which examiners across the banking agencies use. A repeat training finding is therefore a statutory escalation risk, not only an examination comment.

There is also an annual attestation. Under [12 CFR 748.1(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-VII/subchapter-A/part-748/section-748.1), the president or managing official must certify compliance with the requirements of Part 748, which includes 748.2, in the Credit Union Profile each year. That certification is easier to sign with training records that are complete and current.

sections.heading: Can small credit unions share BSA training resources?

blocks.text: Yes. In Letter to Credit Unions [18-CU-04](https://ncua.gov/regulation-supervision/letters-credit-unions-other-guidance/sharing-bank-secrecy-act-resources) (October 2018), the NCUA distributed an interagency statement, developed with the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC and FinCEN, which clarifies that collaborative arrangements to share resources for managing BSA/AML obligations are permissible.

The NCUA's letter says this "may benefit some credit unions, especially smaller institutions which may find hiring or retaining staff with the necessary knowledge a challenge." Shared arrangements still need third-party due diligence, which the letter ties to NCUA Supervisory Letter 07-01. Sharing a training resource does not transfer the obligation: each credit union must still show that its own appropriate personnel were trained on its own policies and risks.

sections.heading: How would the 2026 interagency proposal change credit union BSA training?

blocks.text: It would rename the requirement, raise the bar on keeping training current, and loosen who must approve the program, but it is only a proposal as at November 2026. On April 10, 2026 the OCC, FDIC and NCUA published a [joint proposed rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/10/2026-06948/anti-money-laundering-and-countering-the-financing-of-terrorism-programs) (91 FR 18304) to align their program rules with FinCEN's concurrent proposal.

blocks.text: Two statements in the preamble matter for training design. The agencies say an AML/CFT program "would be more than a one-time creation of an employee training program" and must be kept current as the risk profile changes. They also say training frequency and content "would depend on the bank's ML/TF risk profile and the roles and responsibilities of the persons receiving the training", and acknowledge that non-employees with program roles may need training. A search of the Federal Register found no final rule as at November 2026.

blocks.text: The goal is a record that satisfies an examiner, supports the annual certification, and will still hold if the proposed rule is finalized. The mapping below is illustrative.

blocks.text: For building the roster see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix), and for examination readiness see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit). Credit unions should also run sanctions training alongside BSA training, as described in [OFAC sanctions compliance training](/regulations/ofac-sanctions-compliance-training).

sections.heading: What other training obligations sit alongside BSA training at a credit union?

blocks.text: Consumer compliance training is the other large obligation. The NCUA rates credit unions under the same interagency consumer compliance rating system as banks, which treats training as an assessment factor, covered in [fair lending and UDAAP training](/regulations/fair-lending-and-udaap-training).

Part 748 itself also contains the security program in 748.0 and the 72 hour cyber incident notification duty in 748.1(c), both of which depend on staff knowing what to do. Credit unions with registered mortgage loan originators have separate SAFE Act duties, covered in [SAFE Act mortgage loan originator education](/regulations/safe-act-mortgage-loan-originator-continuing-education). Wider sector context is on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry starts from the credit union's BSA risk assessment and the elements of 748.2, defines what each role must know about the credit union's own procedures, and links each module and assessment to that requirement. If the 2026 proposal is finalized, the change from "appropriate personnel" to an ongoing program becomes a visible update to the framework rather than a rewrite of every course.

faqs.q: Does 12 CFR 748.2 require annual BSA training?
faqs.a: No frequency is stated. The rule requires training for appropriate personnel, and examiners judge whether it is adequate for the credit union's risk. Most credit unions train at least annually, and the 2026 proposal would describe training as ongoing, with frequency set by risk profile and role.

faqs.q: Does the credit union board need BSA training?
faqs.a: The rule requires the board to approve the written BSA program and record that approval in the minutes. To approve it meaningfully, directors need enough knowledge of BSA obligations and the credit union's risks, so board-level BSA briefings are standard practice and are commonly reviewed by examiners.

faqs.q: Who is "appropriate personnel" for credit union BSA training?
faqs.a: The rule does not define it. In practice it covers anyone whose duties touch BSA obligations: member-facing staff, account opening, lending, payments operations, the BSA officer, auditors and the board. The 2026 proposal acknowledges that non-employees with program roles may also need training.

faqs.q: Has the NCUA finalized its new AML/CFT program rule?
faqs.a: No. The NCUA, OCC and FDIC proposed it on April 10, 2026, and comments closed on June 9, 2026. As at November 2026 no final rule had been published, so the current 748.2 wording, "provide training for appropriate personnel", still applies.
